newsitem.title: KAZAKHSTAN: Turkmens, Kazakhs agree Caspian should be exploited.
newsitem.headline: Turkmens, Kazakhs agree Caspian should be exploited.

text.p: The leaders of resource-rich Kazakhstan and Turkmenistan said on Thursday that they recognised the right of all littoral states on the Caspian Sea to develop offshore oil and gas fields.

"The two sides recognise each other's right and that of all the littoral states to carry out work to develop mineral resources on the sea bed," said a declaration signed by Kazakh President Nursultan Nazarbayev and Turkmen President Saparmurat Niyazov and shown to reporters.
But the declaration did not resolve legal and political questions over ownership of the Caspian's resources, which haunt multi-billion dollar energy projects.

The sea, with huge oil and gas reserves, is the subject of fierce diplomatic and legal quarrels over ownership of offshore wealth, brought about by the appearance of three new states on the Caspian after the collapse of the Soviet Union in 1991.
The sea was first divided up between Iran and the Soviet Union in 1921 and again in 1940.
Billions of dollars in oil revenues ride on arcane arguments over whether the Caspian is a sea or a lake, which would determine how its resources should be divided.
Russia and Iran have argued that the sea is actually a lake and is the common property of all the states surrounding it.

Azerbaijan, Turkmenistan and Kazakhstan, pinning their hopes on oil revenues to underpin their new-found independence, say the Caspian is a sea and should be divided up into sectors and be exploited by each country as such.
Recent Turkmen claims to some Azeri oil fields, including some under development, complicate the issue further.
